papersKept.title: Use of Inotropic Agents in Treatment of Systolic Heart Failure.

page.mentor_intro: In acute decompensated heart failure with a low-output state — hypoperfusion, rising lactate, cool extremities despite adequate filling pressures — intravenous inotropes are the temporary scaffold while the cause is treated. Dobutamine, the beta-agonist workhorse, increases contractility and output at the price of tachyarrhythmia and myocardial oxygen demand; milrinone, a phosphodiesterase-3 inhibitor, adds vasodilation and lusitropy but accumulates in renal dysfunction and causes hypotension; levosimendan, the calcium-sensitising agent with active metabolites, offers catecholamine-independent inotropy suited to the beta-blocked patient. None improve hard outcomes — they are a bridge to recovery, device, or decision.

teaching_points.claim: Inotropes in acute heart failure are indicated for the hypoperfused low-output state (end-organ dysfunction with low cardiac output), not for routine decongestion; they are a bridge to definitive therapy.
Dobutamine provides inotropy and mild vasodilation through beta-agonism, with tachyarrhythmia and increased oxygen demand as principal limitations.

Milrinone offers inotropy plus vasodilation and is useful in pulmonary hypertension contexts, but causes hypotension and requires renal dose adjustment; levosimendan provides calcium-sensitising, catecholamine-independent inotropy with utility in beta-blocked patients.
No inotrope has improved survival in acute heart failure; therapy is temporising, with arrhythmia, ischaemia, and hypotension as the costs that must be monitored.

uncertainties: Whether levosimendan improves outcomes over dobutamine in specific phenotypes (beta-blocked, septic-cardiomyopathy) is unproven.
Optimal weaning sequences and inotrope-free intervals are protocolised rather than evidence-defined.
mcq_angles: Agent selection by phenotype and renal function.
case_hooks: A decompensated-HF patient is cold, confused, and lactate-rising on optimal diuretics; decide on inotrope initiation and agent selection.
A beta-blocked low-output patient needs inotropy; argue for levosimendan over escalating dobutamine.

page.mentor_intro: Intrinsic acute kidney injury is parenchymal failure: the kidney itself is injured, whether by ischaemia-reperfusion (the ischaemic ATN of shock and sepsis), nephrotoxins (aminoglycosides, contrast, cisplatin), pigment (rhabdomyolysis, haemolysis), or interstitial inflammation (drug AIN). It is distinguished from pre-renal azotaemia by its failure to respond to volume and by urinary sediment — muddy-brown casts the classic signature of ischaemic ATN. Management is largely supportive: haemodynamic optimisation without fluid overload, nephrotoxin withdrawal, dose adjustment, and the recognition that recovery, when it comes, takes weeks.

teaching_points.claim: AKI is defined by rising creatinine or falling urine output over hours to days; categorising the cause as pre-renal, intrinsic, or post-renal structures the diagnostic work-up.

Intrinsic AKI subtypes include ischaemic/toxic acute tubular necrosis, pigment nephropathy, and interstitial nephritis; the urinary sediment (muddy-brown granular casts in ATN) and failure to respond to volume help distinguish intrinsic from pre-renal disease.
Management is supportive: treat the cause, withdraw nephrotoxins, adjust drug doses, optimise haemodynamics while avoiding fluid overload, and institute RRT only for absolute indications.
Recovery from intrinsic AKI is slow — tubular regeneration takes weeks — and incomplete recovery leaves CKD, the rationale for nephrotoxin vigilance and follow-up.

uncertainties: No pharmacological therapy (dopamine, fenoldopam, mannitol) has improved outcomes in intrinsic AKI.
Biomarker-guided early differentiation of pre-renal from intrinsic AKI is promising but not practice-changing.
mcq_angles: Sediment and diagnostic clues by subtype.
case_hooks: A septic patient has AKI unresponsive to 48 hours of fluid optimisation with muddy-brown casts; classify and manage.
A crush-injury patient has dark urine and rising creatinine; outline the pigment-nephropathy pathway and prevention.
page.gaps: The retained evidence is AKI-general; verify intrinsic-subtype specifics (pigment, AIN, contrast) against dedicated reviews — cross-reference topics 918 and 961 for interstitial causes.

page.mentor_intro: Antifungal therapy for invasive aspergillosis is anchored by the ESCMID-ECMM-ERS guideline: voriconazole is first-line for most invasive disease, with isavuconazole an equal-alternative and liposomal amphotericin B the alternative when azoles fail or are contraindicated. The pharmacology makes or breaks outcomes: voriconazole's nonlinear kinetics, CYP2C19 genetic variability, and narrow therapeutic window demand therapeutic drug monitoring; posaconazole and itraconazole absorption is erratic without formulations optimised. Resistance surveillance — azole-resistant A. fumigatus — is now a first-order concern shaping empiric choices and requiring susceptibility data.

teaching_points.claim: Voriconazole is first-line therapy for invasive aspergillosis per ESCMID-ECMM-ERS guidance, with isavuconazole an equal alternative and liposomal amphotericin B reserved for intolerance, failure, or resistance.

Therapeutic drug monitoring is essential for voriconazole (nonlinear kinetics, CYP2C19 variability, neurotoxicity at high levels) and recommended for posaconazole/itraconazole; trough-guided dosing improves exposure-target attainment.
Combination antifungal therapy (voriconazole plus an echinocandin) is considered in selected high-risk or refractory cases but lacks definitive outcome superiority.
Azole resistance in A. fumigatus is an escalating threat; susceptibility testing and local-resistance patterns should inform empiric and salvage therapy.

uncertainties: The optimal role and timing of combination antifungal therapy remains unresolved.
Whether newer agents (rezafungin, olorofim) displace current first-line therapy awaits comparative outcome data.
case_hooks: An immunocompromised patient with probable IA has CYP2C19 ultrarapid-metaboliser status; adjust voriconazole management.
An IA patient fails voriconazole therapy on adequate troughs; design salvage therapy using the guideline ladder.
page.gaps: The retained guideline summary is 2017-era; verify against the current ESCMID-ECMM-ERS update before approval.

page.mentor_intro: Candidemia is the commonest invasive fungal disease in hospitals, and its management has two non-negotiables: an echinocandin is first-line empiric therapy (fluconazole reserved for stable, susceptible isolates), and central-line removal plus fundoscopic examination are part of the treatment, not adjuncts to it. The IDSA 2016 update codifies therapy by syndrome — candidemia, candidaemia with neutropenia, and organ-specific disease each have distinct durations and agents. The challenges review frames the modern threats: non-albicans species with reduced azole susceptibility, echninocandin resistance emerging in C. glabrata, and the difficulty of diagnosing deep-seated foci without candidemia.

teaching_points.claim: An echinocandin (caspofungin, micafungin, anidulafungin) is recommended first-line empiric therapy for candidemia; fluconazole is an option for stable patients with susceptible isolates, and step-down to oral fluconazole follows susceptibility.
Source control is integral: central-venous-catheter removal where feasible, and ophthalmological examination to exclude endophthalmitis, are parts of standard candidemia management.
Non-albicans species (C. glabrata, C. parapsilosis, C. tropicalis) now dominate many series with reduced azole susceptibility, driving species-level therapy selection and susceptibility testing.
Treatment duration is typically 14 days from first negative blood culture for candidemia without metastatic foci; longer with endophthalmitis, osteoarticular, or other deep-seated disease.

uncertainties: The optimal role of rapid species-identification and resistance-marker testing in directing early therapy is evolving.
Management of persistent candidemia despite therapy (source exclusion, resistance, immune reconstitution) is individualised.
mcq_angles: First-line agent selection and step-down rules.
Source control: line removal and fundoscopy.
case_hooks: A candidaemic ICU patient has a central line and new visual floaters; sequence therapy, line removal, and ophthalmology.
A stable patient grows fluconazole-susceptible C. albicans from blood; justify step-down to oral therapy and duration.

page.mentor_intro: In the immunocompromised host, invasive fungal infection is a race between diagnostic certainty and disease progression — and the modern strategy treats early. Serum and bronchoalveolar galactomannan, beta-D-glucan, and high-resolution CT's halo sign provide pre-culture evidence; the host's net state of immunosuppression (neutropenia duration, corticosteroid dose, transplant type) sets the pre-test probability. The ICU adds a diagnostic wrinkle: invasive aspergillosis now occurs in non-neutropenic patients — COPD on steroids, cirrhosis, post-influenza — where the classic frameworks fit poorly. Therapy is empiric-to-preemptive, anchored on voriconazole with the echinocandins and the newer agents filling defined niches.

teaching_points.claim: Host-immunosuppression assessment (neutropenia, corticosteroid dose, transplant, haematologic malignancy) drives fungal-risk stratification and the threshold for empiric/preemptive therapy.
Non-culture diagnostics — galactomannan (serum and BAL), beta-D-glucan, and CT halo/infarct patterns — enable earlier diagnosis and preemptive therapy before culture or histology.
Invasive aspergillosis increasingly affects non-neutropenic ICU patients (COPD on steroids, post-influenza, liver failure), challenging classical diagnostic frameworks built on neutropenia.
Voriconazole anchors therapy; echinocandins serve as first-line in selected candidiasis contexts and salvage in aspergillosis, with newer agents expanding the armamentarium.

uncertainties: Optimal thresholds for galactomannan and beta-D-glucan positivity vary by host and specimen.
Whether preemptive (diagnostics-triggered) strategies outperform empiric antifungal therapy in outcomes is incompletely tested.
case_hooks: A neutropenic patient has fever, a halo sign on CT, and a rising serum galactomannan; outline the preemptive-therapy decision.
A COPD patient on high-dose steroids deteriorates with putative bacterial pneumonia unresponsive to antibiotics; consider non-neutropenic invasive aspergillosis.
page.gaps: The retained reviews are 2015-2016 era; verify diagnostics thresholds and the newer-agent landscape against current ECMM guidance before approval.

page.mentor_intro: Invasive pulmonary aspergillosis is the clinical entity — fever, cough, pleuritic pain, and progressive infiltrates in an immunocompromised host — that the antifungal guidelines (topic 973) treat. Diagnosis is probabilistic, staged from possible to probable to proven on host factors, radiology, and mycology; the halo sign on early CT is the radiological signature, later giving way to the air-crescent of recovering lesions. Refractory disease — failure on adequate voriconazole — demands systematic reassessment: adherence and troughs first, resistance and imaging progression next, then salvage with a lipid amphotericin, isavuconazole, or combination approaches, with surgical resection considered for localised disease in fit patients.

teaching_points.claim: IPA diagnosis is staged (possible/probable/proven) combining host factors, radiological features (halo sign, infarct-shaped consolidation), and mycological evidence (galactomannan, culture, BAL microscopy).
Invasive aspergillosis increasingly involves non-fumigatus species with variable antifungal susceptibility; identification to species level and susceptibility testing inform management.

Refractory IPA management follows a sequence: confirm exposure (adherence, trough levels), assess resistance and progression, then salvage with alternative agents (liposomal amphotericin B, isavuconazole), combination therapy, or surgical resection for localised disease.

Severe respiratory infection in the immunocompromised demands systematic identification of the cause — invasive diagnostics (BAL with galactomannan, multiplex PCR) improve targeted therapy in hypoxaemic respiratory failure.

uncertainties: The contribution of surgical resection to outcomes in localised IPA is based on case series rather than trials.
Optimal salvage-therapy sequencing for refractory disease is expert-guided.

page.mentor_intro: Suspected stable angina in women runs on a different track: women present later, with atypical and microvascular-predominant disease, and carry a higher burden of angina with non-obstructive coronary arteries — ANOCA/INOCA affecting nearly half of women undergoing angiography for suspected ischemia. The 2021 AHA/ACC chest-pain guideline explicitly addresses sex-specific pathways: functional testing and CT-angiography selection perform differently by sex, and a negative anatomical test does not end the work-up when microvascular disease is plausible. The modern skill is resisting both errors: dismissing women's chest pain as non-cardiac, and stop investigating once the epicardial arteries look clean.

teaching_points.claim: Women with suspected CAD present with atypical symptoms more often, develop more nonobstructive and microvascular disease, and are under-investigated relative to men — the 2021 AHA/ACC guideline codifies sex-specific diagnostic pathways.

ANOCA/INOCA — angina with non-obstructive coronary arteries — may affect nearly half of patients undergoing invasive angiography for suspected ischemia and encompasses coronary microvascular dysfunction and vasospasm.

Diagnostic-test performance differs by sex; CTA subgroup analysis informs appropriate-use, and a clean epicardial angiogram should prompt functional/microvascular assessment (stress imaging, CFR/IMR where available) rather than reassurance alone.
Investigating women requires the dual framework: exclude obstructive disease with appropriate testing, then actively pursue microvascular and vasospastic mechanisms when symptoms persist.

uncertainties: Optimal diagnostic thresholds and test-selection algorithms for women remain refined by ongoing sex-specific outcome data.
Treatment of confirmed microvascular angina improves symptoms more consistently than outcomes.
mcq_angles: Sex differences in presentation and disease pattern.
Test selection by sex from the AHA/ACC guideline.

page.mentor_intro: Iron deficiency anaemia is a sign before it is a diagnosis: in men and postmenopausal women the mandate is finding the blood loss, which is gastrointestinal until proven otherwise. The BSG guideline structures the work-up — coeliac serology with the ferritin, faecal occult blood and endoscopic evaluation by risk, and small-bowel investigation when upper-and-lower endoscopy is negative — while ferritin thresholds (with transferrin saturation where inflammation blurs the picture) anchor the laboratory diagnosis. Treatment restores the deficit (oral first for most, intravenous when oral fails or urgency dictates — see topic 979) but never substitutes for finding the cause.

teaching_points.claim: In adults without inflammation, ferritin below 45 ng/mL is diagnostic of iron deficiency; ferritin 46-99 ng/mL with transferrin saturation below 20% also confirms deficiency — inflammation raises ferritin and masks deficiency.

Men and postmenopausal women with IDA require gastrointestinal evaluation for occult blood loss; coeliac serology is part of the first-line work-up, and small-bowel investigation follows negative bidirectional endoscopy in ongoing-deficiency cases.
Oral iron is first-line for most stable patients; intravenous iron is reserved for intolerance, malabsorption, ongoing losses exceeding oral absorption, or clinical urgency.
Response is monitored by reticulocyte haemoglobin and haemoglobin rise at 2-4 weeks; failure to respond prompts re-evaluation of adherence, absorption, continued loss, and the original diagnosis.

uncertainties: Optimal small-bowel-imaging pathways (capsule versus MR-enterography versus device-assisted enteroscopy) follow local expertise.
The threshold for IV-first strategies in non-urgent IDA is evolving (see topic 979).
mcq_angles: Ferritin/TSAT diagnostic thresholds and inflammation caveats.
GI work-up sequence by sex and risk.

page.mentor_intro: Intravenous iron has moved from rescue to routine: modern formulations (ferric carboxymaltose, iron derisomaltose, ferumoxytol) deliver a gram of iron in 15-60 minutes with reaction rates that no longer justify inpatient observation. The indications are intolerance or non-response to oral iron, malabsorption, ongoing losses outpacing oral absorption, and urgency — but increasingly also convenience and guaranteed delivery. The distinctive modern safety signal is hypophosphatemia: FCM's FGF-23-mediated phosphate wasting is common, usually transient and subclinical, but symptomatic cases with osteomalacia risk warrant monitoring in high-risk and repeated-dose patients.

teaching_points.claim: IV iron indications: oral intolerance or non-response, malabsorption (IBD, bariatric, coeliac), ongoing losses exceeding oral replacement, and clinical urgency; modern formulations allow rapid high-dose repletion in single or split doses.
Oral iron remains first-line for stable, tolerant patients; IV iron achieves faster and more complete repletion and is increasingly used first-line where speed, certainty, or tolerance favour it.

Ferric carboxymaltose is associated with hypophosphatemia through FGF-23-mediated renal phosphate wasting; systematic review quantifies the risk as frequent, usually transient, but occasionally symptomatic.

Hypophosphatemia risk is higher with repeated doses, low baseline phosphate, and certain formulations; monitoring phosphate in at-risk patients and choosing lower-risk formulations (e.g. derisomaltose) are practical mitigations.

uncertainties: Long-term clinical consequences of repeated FCM-associated hypophosphatemia (bone health) are incompletely defined.
Optimal IV-first versus oral-first strategies by phenotype and health-system cost are evolving.
mcq_angles: FCM hypophosphatemia mechanism and risk factors.

page.mentor_intro: Blood-component modifications exist because transfusions can harm in specific hosts: irradiation prevents the rare and fatal transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease in recipients whose immune systems cannot clear donor lymphocytes — congenital immunodeficiency, haematologic malignancy, stem-cell transplant, directed donations from relatives, and HLA-matched platelets. Leukoreduction reduces febrile non-haemolytic reactions, CMV transmission risk, and HLA-alloimmunisation — near-universal in many systems. Washing removes plasma for the rare severe allergic or IgA-deficiency recipient. Each modification adds cost and delay, so the discipline is matching modification to indication, not applying them by default.

teaching_points.claim: Irradiated cellular components prevent transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease (TA-GVHD), a rare but near-universally fatal complication in recipients who cannot reject donor lymphocytes.

Irradiation indications include congenital cellular immunodeficiency, haematologic malignancy and its treatment, haematopoietic stem-cell transplantation, directed donations from blood relatives, and HLA-matched platelets.
Leukoreduction reduces febrile non-haemolytic transfusion reactions, CMV transmission risk, and HLA-alloimmunisation; many jurisdictions apply it universally while others target by indication.

Washed components (removing plasma) are reserved for severe allergic transfusion reactions and IgA-deficiency with anti-IgA — the modification must match a defined indication because each adds cost and delay.

uncertainties: Whether pathogen-reduction technology will consolidate or replace component-modification strategies is system-dependent.
The precise threshold of immunosuppression warranting irradiation in non-classical indications follows expert consensus.
case_hooks: A stem-cell-transplant recipient needs platelets from an HLA-matched sibling donor; specify the required modification and why.
A patient has recurrent febrile reactions to transfusion; explain the role and mechanism of leukoreduction.
page.gaps: The retained evidence is indication-focused; verify modification policies against national haemovigilance and transfusion-service guidelines before approval.
